Sheets of blotting paper drink the water out of the leaves, corrugated ventilators let a current of warm air run between the layers, and the blotters are changed daily until nothing more comes out. Pressure alone would give a flat brown specimen; it is the steady removal of water that leaves the colour _____.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

questions.passage: A drying room can be brought to a low humidity with refrigeration and heat, but the machinery is expensive and stops when the current does. A tin of self-indicating silica gel does the same work for a small quantity of seed: the gel takes up water vapour until the air in the sealed tin is very dry, and its colour shows when it has taken all it can. For a collector working far from a laboratory the tin's chief merit is its _____.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

Passing steam up through a loosely packed charge instead keeps the plant material off the heated metal altogether. The change was made not to raise the yield but to _____ a fault that no later rectification could remove.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

questions.passage: A pressed plant with no label is a curiosity; a pressed plant with a full label is evidence. The slip glued to the corner of the sheet gives the collector, the number, the day, the parish and the ground the plant was standing in, and every later use of the specimen — mapping a range, dating a flowering, matching a name — draws on that slip rather than on the plant. The plant, on this accounting, is an _____ to its label.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Botanic gardens have exchanged seed by printed list for more than two centuries. Each garden issues a catalogue of what it has ripened that year and may request from any other garden's catalogue in return, with no money passing in either direction. <u>The arrangement survives because a garden's surplus costs it nothing and its wants cost it nothing either.</u> A curator with a spare hundred seeds of a plant nobody else grows loses no advantage by sending ninety of them away.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It concedes a weakness in the exchange that later gardens had to correct.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It compares the exchange with the commercial seed trade of the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It questions whether the catalogues accurately describe what is offered.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It identifies the feature of the exchange that accounts for its persistence.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A germination cabinet held at a steady temperature will fail to sprout seed that germinates readily in a seedbed. Many species respond instead to the swing between a warm day and a cool night, and cabinets are therefore run on a cycle, sixteen hours at one temperature and eight at another. <u>The seed is not measuring warmth; it is measuring change.</u> A constant twenty degrees carries no information about whether the seed is buried deep or lying near the surface, and a daily swing does.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It states the principle that the surrounding sentences illustrate.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It acknowledges a limitation of germination cabinets that the text goes on to accept.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It reports a finding that contradicts the claim made in the first sentence.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It defines a term that the rest of the passage uses in a specialised sense.

questions.stem: According to the text, why was confusion between the two systems particularly serious in dispensing?

questions.passage: Two systems of weight were in daily use in an English shop. Goods over the counter were sold by the avoirdupois ounce, of which there are sixteen to the pound; drugs were compounded by the troy ounce, of which there are twelve. The troy ounce is the heavier of the two, so an ounce of a drug and an ounce of sugar were different quantities, and a dispenser who reached for the wrong set of weights made an error that no arithmetic later in the prescription would reveal.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The troy system was being withdrawn while the avoirdupois system remained in use.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Drugs were sold over the counter in the same shop as ordinary goods.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The two kinds of ounce were so close in weight that a balance could not tell them apart.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The mistake left no trace that the rest of the calculation would expose.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A nineteenth-century botanist who found an interesting plant in quantity would press fifty or a hundred sheets of it, number them identically, and post sets to institutions across Europe. The recipients bound them into their own collections, so a single afternoon's collecting is now represented on shelves in a dozen countries. The practice has an unintended value: when one herbarium burned, as several did in the twentieth century, the sheets it held were seldom unique.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Distributing identical sets of specimens widely had the incidental effect of protecting the material against loss.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Botanists distributed duplicate specimens chiefly in order to guard against fires in herbaria.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Herbarium fires in the twentieth century destroyed most of the specimens collected in the nineteenth.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A specimen is valuable only when the herbarium holding it can show that no copy exists elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the claim that winnowing removed material that screening had left behind?

questions.passage:
Seed arriving from the field carries chaff, dust and broken seed, and a cleaner removes them in stages. A merchant weighed a thousand seeds drawn at random from the same lot after each stage.
Stage of cleaningWeight of 1,000 seeds (grams)
As received27.4
After screening31.9
After winnowing35.6
After gravity table36.1

choices.label: A
choices.content: The weight of a thousand seeds rose at every stage of cleaning.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The weight of a thousand seeds rose from 31.9 grams to 35.6 grams across the winnowing stage.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The weight of a thousand seeds was lowest, at 27.4 grams, in the lot as received.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The weight of a thousand seeds rose by only 0.5 grams across the gravity table.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the claim that most of a lavender charge's oil comes over early in the run?

Distillers of lavender disagree about how long a charge should be run. A grower kept the still going for four hours on one charge and recorded the oil collected in each hour separately, obtaining the results shown.
Hour of the runOil collected in that hour (millilitres)

Second96

Fourth9

choices.label: A
choices.content: The fourth hour yielded 9 millilitres, the smallest quantity recorded in the run.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The oil collected fell in every hour of the run after the first.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The second hour yielded 96 millilitres, which is more than the third and fourth hours together.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The first hour yielded 310 millilitres, more than twice the total collected in the remaining three hours.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the chemist's proposal?

questions.passage: Oil of peppermint has long been diluted with cheaper material before sale. A pure oil rotates the plane of polarised light through a characteristic angle, and mixtures do not, so a polarimeter reading has been used as a check on purity since the nineteenth century. A chemist proposes that the reading cannot by itself establish that a sample is unadulterated.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Some adulterated samples show a rotation far outside the range expected of pure oil.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Two different diluents, added together in the right proportions, leave the sample's rotation unchanged from that of the pure oil.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The rotation of pure peppermint oil varies slightly with the temperature at which it is measured.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Polarimeters manufactured before 1900 were less precise than modern instruments.

questions.passage: A herbarium sheet records the day a plant was in flower at a named place, and collectors have been writing that date on labels for two hundred years. Researchers comparing the flowering dates on old sheets with dates recorded today have found the two sets separated by a fortnight or more for many species. The comparison works only because the collectors were not thinking about the question at all: a date written down to identify a specimen carries none of the expectations that would attach to a date written down to _____

choices.label: D

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

questions.passage: Every pure essential oil bends a ray of light passing through it by a fixed amount at a given temperature, and the instrument that measures this takes a single drop and reads in seconds. The figure it returns will not name what has been added to a sample, and two different adulterants may push the reading in opposite directions. A refractometer reading is therefore best understood as a way of _____

choices.label: B

questions.stem: The student wants to explain to a general audience what the garden added to the students' textbooks. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Medical students in the sixteenth century learned drugs from written descriptions.
  • A description could be matched to more than one plant growing in the field.
  • University physic gardens grew named plants in labelled beds for students to see.
  • A demonstrator walked the beds with the class and named each plant aloud.
  • Students who had walked the beds could recognise the plants when they later prescribed them.

choices.label: A
choices.content: University physic gardens grew named plants in labelled beds, and a demonstrator walked the beds with the class and named each plant aloud.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Medical students in the sixteenth century learned drugs from written descriptions, and students who had walked the beds could recognise the plants later.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A description could be matched to more than one plant growing in the field, and students learned drugs from written descriptions.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Because a written description could fit more than one plant growing in the field, the labelled beds and the demonstrator who named each plant aloud gave students a direct acquaintance with the drug plants that they could carry into practice.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain to a general audience how a loan benefits the lending herbarium. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A herbarium lends specimens to researchers at other institutions.
  • Loans travel between institutions rather than to individuals.
  • The borrowing institution takes responsibility for the sheets while they are held.
  • A specialist revising a group may borrow several hundred sheets at once.
  • Sheets returned from loan often carry a new determination slip added by the specialist.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A specialist revising a group may borrow several hundred sheets at once and often returns them with a new determination slip attached, so the lending herbarium gets its material named by an expert it does not employ.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Loans travel between institutions rather than to individuals, and the borrowing institution takes responsibility for the sheets while they are held.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A herbarium lends specimens to researchers at other institutions, and a specialist may borrow several hundred sheets at once.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Sheets returned from loan often carry a new determination slip added by the specialist, and loans travel between institutions rather than to individuals.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain to a general audience why the envelope is worth the trouble of attaching. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Loose seeds, fallen petals and broken fragments cannot be glued to a sheet.
  • A small paper envelope is fixed to a corner of the sheet to hold them.
  • The envelope carries the same number as the specimen.
  • Material from the envelope can be examined under a microscope and returned.
  • Seeds from such envelopes have been germinated a century after collection.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Material from the envelope can be examined under a microscope and returned, and the envelope carries the same number as the specimen.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The envelope keeps loose seeds and fragments with the specimen that produced them, and because material can be taken out, examined under a microscope and put back, seeds from such envelopes have even been germinated a century after collection.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A small paper envelope is fixed to a corner of the sheet and carries the same number as the specimen.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Loose seeds, fallen petals and broken fragments cannot be glued to a sheet, so a small paper envelope is fixed to a corner.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

questions.passage: When a botanist publishes a new species, one pressed specimen is designated as the permanent point of reference for the name. Later workers who disagree about what the name covers do not argue from descriptions, which are always incomplete, but go back to that sheet. The specimen settles nothing about how wide the species should be drawn; it settles only which plant the name is anchored to, which is a smaller question and a far more answerable one.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

A laminate of aluminium foil between two plastic films does not, and a seam heat-sealed across it does not either. The packet does not dry the seed. It takes in heat all day and gives it back through the night, so the air within a few feet of it never falls as far as the air in the open ground beyond. Gardeners planted apricots and figs against such walls in counties where those trees will not set fruit otherwise, and the plants were not hardier there; the frost simply reached them later and left them sooner.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Gardeners in cold counties abandoned tender fruit once open-ground varieties became available.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A wall extends the growing season next to it by moderating night temperatures rather than by altering the plants.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

questions.stem: According to the text, why do herbaria not preserve all their material in spirit?

questions.passage: A pressed orchid flower is a brown smear, and a pressed fungus is worse. Herbaria therefore keep a second, wet collection: the flower or the fruiting body goes whole into a jar of spirit, where it holds its shape and something of its colour indefinitely. The jars take a hundred times the shelf space of a sheet and cannot be posted, so nothing goes into spirit that would survive the press, and the two collections between them cover what neither could cover alone.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The cost of spirit rose beyond what most herbaria could afford.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Pressed sheets record collecting data that jars have no room to carry.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Spirit collections demand far more space and cannot be sent through the post.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Specimens kept in spirit lose their colour more quickly than pressed ones do.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain to an audience unfamiliar with perfumery why clary sage became a field crop. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Clary sage yields an oil containing sclareol.
  • Sclareol can be converted into a substance with the fixing properties of ambergris.
  • Ambergris comes from sperm whales and was scarce and costly.
  • A fixative slows the evaporation of the lighter parts of a perfume.
  • Clary sage is grown as a field crop in France, Russia and the United States.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Clary sage is grown as a field crop in France, Russia and the United States, and its oil contains sclareol.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Ambergris comes from sperm whales and was scarce and costly, and a fixative slows the evaporation of the lighter parts of a perfume.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Sclareol can be converted into a substance with the fixing properties of ambergris, which comes from sperm whales.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Clary sage is grown on a field scale because its oil contains sclareol, which can be converted into a substitute for the scarce and costly whale product ambergris, a fixative that slows the evaporation of a perfume's lighter parts.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain to an audience unfamiliar with propagation why layering succeeds with difficult species. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Layering roots a shoot while it is still attached to the parent plant.
  • A shoot is bent to the ground, wounded on its underside and pegged under soil.
  • The parent continues to supply the shoot with water until roots form.
  • A cutting, by contrast, is severed first and must survive on its own reserves.
  • Layering is slower than taking cuttings but succeeds with species that root poorly.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Because a layered shoot stays attached to its parent and goes on being supplied with water while it roots, it is not thrown onto its own reserves as a severed cutting is, which is why layering succeeds with species that root poorly.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Layering is slower than taking cuttings, and a shoot is bent to the ground, wounded on its underside and pegged under soil.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A cutting is severed first and must survive on its own reserves, while a layered shoot is bent to the ground and pegged under soil.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Species that root poorly are propagated by layering, a method in which a shoot is wounded on its underside before being pegged down.

questions.stem: The student wants to present a balanced account of the abbreviated Latin used on prescriptions. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Prescriptions were written in abbreviated Latin until well into the twentieth century.
  • The abbreviations covered the drug, the quantity, the form and the timing of a dose.
  • A dispenser anywhere in Europe could read a prescription written in another country.
  • A patient reading the same prescription could not.
  • Some of the abbreviations were similar enough to be confused with one another.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The abbreviations gave the drug, the quantity, the form and the timing compactly enough that a dispenser anywhere in Europe could read a prescription written abroad, though the patient could not and some of the abbreviations were similar enough to be confused.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Prescriptions were written in abbreviated Latin until well into the twentieth century, and the abbreviations covered the drug, the quantity, the form and the timing of a dose.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Some of the abbreviations were similar enough to be confused with one another, and a patient reading a prescription could not understand it.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A dispenser anywhere in Europe could read a prescription written in another country, because prescriptions were written in abbreviated Latin.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A tincture can be made by steeping the drug in spirit for days and then straining, or by letting spirit trickle slowly down through a packed column of it. Steeping stops when the liquid and the drug reach a balance and no more will come out. Percolation never reaches that balance, because fresh spirit is always arriving at the top, and the difference in strength between the two products is therefore _____ rather than accidental.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Most seeds can be dried to a few per cent of their weight in water and stored for decades. The seeds of oaks, horse chestnuts and many rainforest trees cannot: dry them below about a quarter of their fresh weight and they die outright, so a store that would preserve wheat for a century destroys an acorn in a fortnight. For these species the standard method of conservation is not merely ineffective but _____.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: An apothecary's scale ran in grains, twenty grains to the scruple and three scruples to the drachm, and a dispenser weighing out a powerful drug worked at the bottom of that ladder. A difference of two or three grains in a dose meant nothing in a mild preparation and a great deal in a strong one, so the same balance and the same weights were used with a care that looked _____ to anyone who did not know which drug was on the pan.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Sowing a sample and counting the seedlings answers the question of viability in a fortnight or more, and for a species that must first be chilled it can take a season. Soaking a cut seed in a colourless salt of tetrazolium answers it in a few hours instead: living tissue reduces the salt to a red dye and dead tissue stays pale, so the embryo reports its own condition. The test does not improve on sowing for accuracy; what it offers is _____.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

It must first pass some weeks cold and damp, a condition the seed meets under snow and the nurseryman supplies in a box of moist sand in a cold shed. questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The tall waisted jar of tin-glazed earthenware that stood on an apothecary's shelf is now prized for its painted decoration, but the panel that matters is the plain band across its belly. On it the contents were written in abbreviated Latin, and because the glaze could be scraped and repainted the band could be rewritten when the jar was given to another drug. <u>The jar was designed to outlast any particular thing put into it.</u>

choices.label: A
choices.content: It shifts the discussion from the jar's decoration to its manufacture.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It draws a conclusion from the rewritable label the passage has just described.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It introduces an objection to the value collectors place on the jars.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It provides an example of the abbreviated Latin used on the band.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Rose petals give up their oil grudgingly, and a first distillation leaves much of the most fragrant material dissolved in the water that comes over with it. Distillers therefore return that water to the still and pass it through a second time, sometimes with a fresh charge of petals in it. The practice recovers oil that would otherwise be poured away, and it also concentrates the water itself into the rose water sold as a product in its own right.

choices.label: A
choices.content: To explain a step in rose distilling and identify the two benefits it yields

choices.label: B
choices.content: To argue that rose water is more valuable than the oil recovered alongside it

choices.label: C
choices.content: To trace the history of rose distilling from its origins to the present day

choices.label: D
choices.content: To compare the yields obtained by distillers working in different regions

questions.stem: According to the text, what is the practical value of the two rules?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Two rules of thumb have guided seed storage since the 1960s. Each one per cent reduction in the moisture content of a seed roughly doubles the time it will remain alive, and so does each fall of about five degrees Celsius in the storage temperature. The rules hold only within limits — below about five per cent moisture further drying stops helping and may harm — but within those limits they let a store predict the effect of a change before making it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: They show that drying seed is beneficial no matter how far it is taken.

choices.label: B
choices.content: They allow the effect of a change in storage conditions to be estimated in advance.

choices.label: C
choices.content: They identify the single storage condition that matters more than any other.

choices.label: D
choices.content: They establish the exact number of years a given seed lot will remain alive.

questions.stem: According to the text, what is the consequence of cutting a peppermint crop early?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The peppermint plant makes its oil in glands on the leaf, and the composition of that oil changes as the season advances. Early in flowering the oil is high in menthone, which smells sharp and slightly bitter; as flowering proceeds the menthone is progressively converted to menthol, which gives the cooling character the crop is grown for. A grower who cuts too early loses nothing in weight of oil and a great deal in what buyers will pay for it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The plants regrow more slowly and yield less at the following cutting.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The oil obtained contains no menthol at all and cannot be sold.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The oil obtained is worth less because less of its menthone has become menthol.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The oil obtained is smaller in quantity because the glands are not yet full.

questions.stem: Which quotation from the daily book most effectively illustrates the historians' claim?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The head gardener of a physic garden kept a daily book through the winter of 1837, recording the temperature of each glasshouse at seven in the morning together with what he had done to the flues the night before. Historians of horticulture have used the book to argue that he was managing the houses to a target rather than simply keeping them from freezing.

choices.label: A
choices.content: “Stove at 62 this morning, three degrees above what I want it; damped the flue at ten last night and shall damp it earlier tonight.”

choices.label: B
choices.content: “Hard frost again, and the water in the tank frozen an inch thick by morning.”

choices.label: C
choices.content: “The new house is finished, and the glazier has left his ladder against the orangery.”

choices.label: D
choices.content: “Fired the stove late, the wind being in the east and the night bitter.”

questions.stem: Which quotation from the journal most effectively supports that argument?

questions.passage: A collector sent to south-west China in the 1900s was instructed to bring back living plants as well as pressed specimens. His field journal has been used to argue that he chose what to collect by what he judged would survive the journey rather than by what was botanically novel.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the botanist's proposal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A plant now confined to a few sites in the north of England is listed in county floras of the 1850s from parishes where it has not been seen since. A botanist proposes that herbarium sheets can settle whether the plant has genuinely retreated or was simply misidentified by the earlier recorders.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The county floras of the 1850s were compiled by recorders who rarely travelled outside their own parishes.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The plant is difficult to distinguish in the field from a commoner relative.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Modern surveys of the northern sites find the plant in smaller numbers each decade.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Sheets collected in those southern parishes in the 1850s, re-examined today, are correctly named and carry full locality data.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

questions.passage: Jasmine and tuberose give almost nothing to a still. The compounds that carry their scent are destroyed at the temperature distillation requires, and what survives smells little like the flower. Perfumers therefore laid the blossoms on trays of purified fat, which absorbs the scent as the flowers continue to give it off, renewing the flowers daily for weeks before washing the fat with spirit. The method is laborious and was kept in use for as long as it was because, for these flowers, it _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: allowed the flowers to be stored before processing.

choices.label: B
choices.content: preserved a scent that heat would have ruined.

choices.label: C
choices.content: produced a larger quantity of oil than distillation.

choices.label: D
choices.content: required less skilled labour than distillation did.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

questions.passage: Plants from high mountains die in ordinary garden soil more often from wet than from cold. In their own ground they spend the winter under snow, dry at the neck, with meltwater draining instantly away through broken rock. A bed built for them is therefore made mostly of stone chippings with very little soil among them, an arrangement that looks starved and is in fact chosen because it _____

choices.content: lets water leave the root as fast as it arrives.

choices.label: B
choices.content: holds warmth around the root through the winter.

choices.label: C
choices.content: supplies the minerals such plants take from rock.

choices.label: D
choices.content: prevents the plants from growing beyond their natural size.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain to a general audience why provenance data must be recorded in the field. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A wild-collected seed lot is recorded with the exact place, altitude and habitat of collection.
  • Two lots of the same species from different valleys may differ in cold tolerance.
  • A lot without collection data cannot be matched to a site for reintroduction.
  • Provenance data are recorded at the moment of collection and cannot be recovered later.
  • Some older collections in store carry only a country name.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Two lots of the same species from different valleys may differ in cold tolerance, and a lot without collection data cannot be matched to a site for reintroduction.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A wild-collected seed lot is recorded with the exact place, altitude and habitat of collection, and provenance data are recorded at the moment of collection.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Provenance data cannot be recovered once the collector has left the site, and without the exact place, altitude and habitat a lot cannot be matched to a site for reintroduction — which matters because two lots of one species from different valleys may differ in cold tolerance.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Some older collections in store carry only a country name, and a wild-collected seed lot is recorded with the exact place, altitude and habitat of collection.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain to a general audience why double flowers support fewer insects. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A garden planted only with showy double-flowered varieties supports few insects.
  • Double flowers have extra petals in place of the parts that make pollen and nectar.
  • Single-flowered forms of the same species carry both.
  • A survey of one garden found four times as many bee visits to single-flowered beds.
  • Many gardeners now keep a proportion of single-flowered forms for this reason.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Gardens planted only with showy double-flowered varieties support few insects, and many gardeners now keep a proportion of single-flowered forms.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Single-flowered forms of a species carry both pollen and nectar, and double flowers have extra petals.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Double flowers carry extra petals in place of the parts that produce pollen and nectar, so they offer insects nothing to collect; one garden survey counted four times as many bee visits to beds of single-flowered forms, which retain both.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A survey of one garden found four times as many bee visits to single-flowered beds, and many gardeners now keep a proportion of single-flowered forms.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasise how a distiller turns a disposal cost into something useful. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The plant material left in a still at the end of a run is called the spent charge.
  • It holds no more oil, but it is bulky and wet, and a works must move it daily.
  • Lavender stalks are spread to dry and then burnt under the boiler.
  • Spent rose petals are carted back to the fields and ploughed in.
  • A works that has no use for the spent charge pays a contractor to take it away.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A works that has no use for the spent charge pays a contractor to take it away, and the spent charge must be moved daily.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Rather than pay a contractor to take away a bulky wet material that holds no more oil, a distiller dries the lavender stalks and burns them under the boiler and ploughs the spent rose petals back into the fields.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The plant material left in a still at the end of a run is called the spent charge, and it holds no more oil but is bulky and wet.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Lavender stalks are spread to dry and then burnt under the boiler, and spent rose petals are carted back to the fields and ploughed in.
